title: USP-NF General Chapter <1154> Liposome Drug Products
text: Liposomes have a lipid bilayer and an aqueous compartment. The aqueous compartment and lipid bilayer provide distinct locations for incorporating water-soluble and lipophilic payloads. Product-specific characterization depends on the formulation and route.
limitation: General formulation guidance. Provides neither a drug-specific ratio nor a performance prediction.

title: Drug Delivery through Liposomes
text: Liposome design considers lipid composition, vesicle characteristics, and drug association with aqueous or lipid regions.
limitation: Background for candidate design. Independently measured outcomes are needed for a particular batch.

title: Eugster et al. (2024), Leveraging machine learning to streamline the development of liposomal drug delivery systems
text: The study related liposome formation and size to chip geometry, lipid composition and microfluidic flow settings. Its size regression used a screened subset of runs.
limitation: This is the training source for the Eugster model. It cannot independently confirm that model or establish drug-specific loading, release or tissue delivery.

title: Bragagni et al. (2012), Comparative study of liposomes, transfersomes and ethosomes for topical celecoxib
text: The study compared liposomes, transfersomes and ethosomes for topical celecoxib. The Tween 20 ethosome was a favorable experimental candidate in this comparison.
limitation: Study-specific comparison using excised human skin. Batch F measurements apply to that published formulation.

title: Shahiwala et al. (2023), Designing Optimum Drug Delivery Systems Using Machine Learning Approaches: a Prototype Study of Niosomes
text: The authors examined surfactant and cholesterol ratios and validated a formulation model with experimental donepezil hydrochloride niosomes.
limitation: A carrier- and drug-specific example. It does not justify transferring a ratio across drug forms or administration routes.

title: Ascenso et al. (2015), Development, characterization, and skin delivery studies of ultradeformable vesicles
text: The experimental comparison varied surfactants in transfersomes and included ethanol-containing vesicle systems for skin delivery. It studied caffeine and vitamin E as model actives.
limitation: Evidence for the studied model actives and skin experiments. Results do not transfer directly to a different payload.

title: Riva et al. (2019), Improved Oral Absorption of Quercetin from Quercetin Phytosome
text: The study evaluated a lecithin-based quercetin phytosome and reported oral bioavailability in healthy volunteers.
limitation: Oral pharmacokinetics for a specific product. It does not establish release kinetics, tissue targeting, or efficacy for another formulation.

title: Yanes et al. (2025), Making in vitro release and formulation data AI-ready
text: The liposome release database records formulation and assay conditions alongside digitized curves. Release comparisons require defined medium, apparatus and test conditions.
limitation: A 24-hour measurement is not a full release curve. Results from incompatible assays are not direct substitutes.

title: FDA (2018), Liposome Drug Products guidance
text: The guidance discusses liposome product characterization and separates chemistry, manufacturing and controls from pharmacokinetics and bioavailability evidence.
limitation: General guidance. It does not establish delivery to a target tissue for an untested formulation.

title: Liposome—A Comprehensive Approach for Researchers
text: This open-access chapter surveys liposome preparation and characterization. It identifies particle size, polydispersity, surface charge, encapsulation, solubility and lamellarity as formulation attributes that require measurement and method-specific interpretation.
limitation: General preparation and characterization context only. It does not establish a drug-specific estimate or predict a new batch.

title: Niosomes as Carrier in Dermal Drug Delivery
text: This open-access chapter describes dermal niosomes as non-ionic surfactant vesicles commonly combined with cholesterol. Hydrophilic and lipophilic compounds can associate with different vesicle regions; topical performance depends on the drug, composition and skin-barrier conditions.
limitation: Review background for dermal formulation design. It supplies no validated prediction for a requested drug or batch.

title: Ethosomes: An Exciting and Promising Alcoholic Carrier System for Treating Androgenic Alopecia
text: This open-access chapter reviews ethosomes made from phospholipids, ethanol and water, with optional co-solvents or modifiers. It discusses preparation and characterization and explains that ethanol, composition and drug properties can affect vesicle size and skin permeation.
limitation: The reported examples and mechanisms are formulation-specific background. They do not support a celecoxib or other new-batch numerical prediction.

title: Hydrogels and Their Combination with Liposomes, Niosomes, or Transfersomes for Dermal and Transdermal Drug Delivery
text: This open-access chapter reviews liposomes, niosomes and transfersomes used alone or with hydrogel vehicles. It describes formulation-dependent skin permeation, local-depot and release considerations and emphasizes that the carrier and gel conditions define the experiment.
limitation: Cross-carrier review context only. It does not validate a ranking, tissue-targeting estimate or release prediction for a new formulation.

title: Phytosomes as a Novel Approach to Drug Delivery System
text: This open-access chapter describes phytosomes as complexes formed between phospholipids and plant-derived constituents. It summarizes formulation and bioavailability context for selected botanical actives.
limitation: Botanical phospholipid-complex background only. Results for a plant constituent do not establish a synthetic-drug estimate or formulation ratio.

title: Topical and Transdermal Drug Delivery: From Simple Potions to Smart Technologies
text: This review distinguishes topical and transdermal carrier classes, including transfersomes, ethosomes and niosomes, and discusses skin-barrier pathways. The delivery mechanism and outcome depend on carrier composition, drug properties and route conditions.
limitation: Class-level review context, not a matched-drug observation or a quantitative tissue-delivery prediction.

title: Current Advances in Specialised Niosomal Drug Delivery: Manufacture, Characterization and Drug Delivery Applications
text: This review covers niosome manufacture, characterization and drug-delivery applications. It summarizes how surfactant choice, composition and preparation methods shape the properties measured for individual formulations.
limitation: Review evidence is contextual; measurements from different drugs, recipes and assays are not interchangeable or predictions for a new batch.

title: Lipid-Based Drug Delivery Systems: Concepts and Recent Advances in Transdermal Applications
text: This review surveys lipid-based topical and transdermal carriers and their formulation approaches. It presents carrier composition, preparation and reported outcomes as study-specific evidence rather than one transferable performance profile.
limitation: A cross-carrier review cannot validate ranking or tissue targeting for an unseen drug; compare only measurements with compatible conditions and assays.

title: Phytosomal Delivery of Natural Bioactives: Advancing Bioavailability, Targeted Drug Delivery, and Clinical Translation
text: This recent review summarizes phytosome formulation and characterization for natural bioactives. It highlights variability in particle size, PDI, entrapment and release across compounds, compositions and preparation methods.
limitation: Review-level botanical evidence only. It does not establish a drug-specific numerical estimate or prove tissue targeting for another formulation.
